newsitem.title: GREECE: PRESS DIGEST - GREEK FINANCIAL NEWS- NOV 18.
newsitem.headline: PRESS DIGEST - GREEK FINANCIAL NEWS- NOV 18.

text.p: Leading stories in the Greek financial press:

--The new taxes to support the 1997 budget have been decided and will be announced tomorrow. National Economy and Finance Minister Yannos Papandoniou hopes the new measures will raise 300 billion drachmas, a third of the increase in revenues forecast for the new budget. Achievement of budget targets will also be supported by the increased growth rate, with GDP hoped to rise by 3.3 percent, the containment of public expenditures to 8.5 percent and the more effective management of the public debt.

--Interest and amortization for the new budget will total 7.5 trillion drachmas, amounting for the lion's share of revenues, expected to not exceed 8.5 trillion. The high costs of servicing the public debt are the Achilles' heel of the budge and the economy.

--The budget goes through its hoops today as ruling party PASOK MPs and the party's Central Committee convene to discuss the government's economic policy. The meeting is expected to be an opportunity for dissenters - many of them representing the views of senior party members bound not to speak by a 'gentleman's agreement' - to air their views.

--Papandoniou is to meet with president of the Association of Athens Stock Exchange Members (SMEHA) Panagiotis Kondalexis today and discuss the details of how to cover Delta Securities' 2.6 billion default to the clearing house and new regulations on trading in light of the scandal.
--Another 10 insurance firms face closure as they fail to meet reserve fund guidelines. The development ministry has so far approved the continued operation of only 20 firms.

--Many smaller brokerage firms - uninvolved in the speculation that led to the closure of the Athens bourse late week - will be forced to close, as the government plans to significantly increase capital requirements for brokerage firms.

--Prime Minister Costas Simitis is expected to announce interest of 7.5 percent on all new bond issues, and 15 percent on derivatives as well as the revision of taxation of mutual funds. The government has adopted the dogma of 'tax whatever moves' after consultations with European Union experts and international financial houses.
--The judicial inquiry into last week's developments at the Athens Stock Exchange is expected to soon throw light on the backstage dealings at the bourse and name names.
--Following the Cabinet meeting on Tuesday, the prime minister will explain the details of his economic policy, assisted by Papandoniou.
--The continuing shipping fuel scam has meant losses of one billion drachmas a month to the Greek state. --Maria Petrakis, Athens Newsroom +301 3311812-4
